theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Function names are those used in common spreadsheet programs; where two are given (for example VLOOKUP or XLOOKUP), either is accepted. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Function names are those used in common spreadsheet programs; where two are given, either is accepted. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: A formula in a cash-flow sheet divides each month's costs by the number of guests, and one month's guest cell is blank. Which error value appears?
What symbol is placed before a column letter or row number to make that part of a cell reference absolute?
Cells B2 to B5 hold 1,200, 850, 0 and 450. What does =SUM(B2:B5) return?
Cells C2 to C6 hold 12, 18, an empty cell, 30 and 20. What does =AVERAGE(C2:C6) return?
Cells D2 to D5 hold 45, 12, 78 and 33. What does =MAX(D2:D5)-MIN(D2:D5) return?
Name a function that finds a value in the first column of a table and returns a value from another column in the same row.
Which function counts the cells in a range that are not empty, whether they hold numbers or text?
What is the term for a set of recorded steps that can be replayed to repeat a task in a spreadsheet automatically?
What error value is shown when a formula contains a misspelt function name, such as =SUMM(A1:A5)?
Cells A2 to A6 hold Bar, Kitchen, Bar, Rooms and Bar. Cells C2 to C6 hold 1,500, 2,000, 2,500, 3,000 and 500. What does =SUMIF(A2:A6,"Bar",C2:C6) return?
Cell B2 holds 64,000. A formula pays 5% of B2 if B2 is 50,000 or more, and 0 if it is not. What does it return?
A manager saves one file that holds a budget sheet, an actuals sheet and a summary sheet. What is that file called in spreadsheet terms?
What type of chart plots pairs of values to show whether two measures, such as price and number sold, are related?
Cell A2 holds last year's sales of J$800,000 and B2 holds this year's J$920,000. What does =(B2-A2)/A2 show when formatted as a percentage?

essays.stem: Plan the design of a workbook to track a hotel's monthly budget against actual spending for six departments, so that the general manager can see problems quickly.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by agreeing the purpose with the general manager: to compare budget and actual spending each month, by department and by cost line, and flag any line more than 10% over budget. The users are the six department heads, who enter or check figures, and the general manager, who reads the summary. I would plan separate sheets: a settings sheet with the department list, the cost codes and the 10% threshold as named cells; a budget sheet with the approved monthly figures; an actuals sheet with the monthly spend imported from the accounts system as a table; a summary sheet that uses SUMIFS to total budget and actual by department and month, works out the variance and percentage, and uses IF to show 'Over' or 'OK'; and a chart sheet. Conditional formatting would turn lines over the threshold red. Input cells would be unlocked and the rest protected, with data validation for departments. A notes sheet would explain the purpose, sources, formulas and owner. I would test it with known figures before use and keep a version log.
markingPoints: Agrees the purpose, users, inputs and outputs
Plans separate input, calculation and output sheets
Uses suitable functions, such as SUMIFS and IF, with named settings
Uses conditional formatting, validation and protection
Documents and tests the workbook before use

essays.stem: Explain how a lookup function (VLOOKUP or XLOOKUP, or INDEX with MATCH) can be used to bring prices from a price list into an order sheet, and describe the common mistakes and how to avoid them.
essays.modelAnswer: The price list would be kept as a table with a unique product code in one column and the price in another. On the order sheet, a lookup formula would take the product code typed on each line, search the code column of the price list and return the price from the same row. With VLOOKUP, the codes must be in the first column of the range, and the formula gives the column number of the price and FALSE for an exact match. XLOOKUP, or INDEX with MATCH, lets the price column be anywhere and does not break if columns are inserted. Common mistakes include leaving the match type as approximate, which gives wrong prices without any warning; codes stored as text in one place and numbers in another; extra spaces, which TRIM can remove; duplicate codes in the list; and relative references to the table, which shift when copied, so the range should be absolute or a named table. Missing codes give #N/A, which IFERROR can turn into 'Code not found'. I would test the sheet with known codes and prices.
markingPoints: Sets up the price list with unique codes as the lookup table
Explains how the lookup finds the code and returns the price
Notes the need for an exact match and the column structure
Identifies other common mistakes, such as text and number codes, spaces, duplicates or shifting ranges
Uses IFERROR or similar for missing codes and tests the result

essays.stem: Compare using formulas such as SUMIF or SUMIFS with using a pivot table to summarise a year of sales data, and recommend when to use each.
essays.modelAnswer: Formulas such as SUMIFS calculate totals that meet one or more conditions, such as sales for Ocho Rios in March. They update at once when the data changes, can be placed exactly where a fixed report layout needs them, and can be linked to other calculations, such as variances against a budget. However, each total needs its own formula, so a large summary takes time to build, and formula errors are easy to make and hard to spot. A pivot table summarises the whole list by dragging fields, such as branch, month and product, into rows, columns and values. It is quick to build, easy to change to look at the data in new ways, can show counts, averages and percentages, and can be filtered or drilled into. Its limits are that it must be refreshed when the data changes, its layout can shift, and it is harder to link into a fixed report. I would use a pivot table to explore the data and find patterns, and SUMIFS formulas for a fixed monthly report that others rely on.
markingPoints: Explains how SUMIF or SUMIFS formulas summarise data
Gives the strengths and weaknesses of the formula approach
Explains how a pivot table summarises data
Gives the strengths and weaknesses of pivot tables, including refreshing
Makes a clear recommendation of when to use each

essays.stem: Describe how you would check that a complex spreadsheet used for management decisions is accurate before and during its use.
essays.modelAnswer: Before use, I would check the design against the purpose, then test the formulas with a small set of test data where I already know the answers, including unusual cases such as zero values, blanks, very large figures and missing codes. I would check that totals cross-cast, so the sum of the rows equals the sum of the columns. I would use the formula auditing tools, such as showing formulas and tracing precedents, to check that ranges cover all rows and that copied formulas have the correct absolute and relative references. I would look for hard-typed numbers inside formulas and move them into labelled input cells. A colleague would review the workbook independently. During use, imported data would be checked with control totals, such as the number of records and the total value, against the source system. Data validation and protection would reduce input errors, and check cells could flag when totals do not agree. Each version would be saved with a log of changes, and any change to formulas would be tested again before use.
markingPoints: Tests formulas with known data, including unusual cases
Uses cross-casting and auditing tools to check ranges and references
Removes hard-typed numbers and gets an independent review
Checks imported data with control totals and uses validation and check cells
Controls versions and retests after changes

essays.stem: Explain how to choose and design charts that present spreadsheet data clearly and honestly to senior managers.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would decide the one message each chart must show, then choose the chart type that suits it. A line chart suits trends over time, such as monthly sales; a column or bar chart suits comparisons between groups, such as branches; a pie chart suits shares of a whole, but only with a few parts; and a scatter chart shows whether two measures are related. The chart should have a clear title that states the message, labelled axes with units such as J$ or %, and a legend only if needed. I would remove clutter such as 3-D effects, heavy gridlines and many colours, and use one strong colour to pick out the key item. To be honest, the value axis of a column chart should start at zero, or any break should be clearly marked, and the same scales should be used when charts are compared. The data source and date should be shown. I would check every chart against the figures in the table, and test that it can be read in black and white and by people with colour blindness.
markingPoints: Decides the message first and chooses a suitable chart type
Gives correct uses of line, column, pie and scatter charts
Uses clear titles, labels, units and minimal clutter
Keeps charts honest: zero baselines or marked breaks and consistent scales
Shows the source and checks the chart against the data

essays.stem: A workbook holds the salaries, bank details and appraisal ratings of 60 staff. Explain how you would protect it, with reference to the general aims of the data protection law.
essays.modelAnswer: This workbook holds personal data that could harm staff if it were seen or misused, so the data protection law's general aims apply: collect only what is needed, use it only for its purpose, keep it accurate and secure, and keep it no longer than needed. I would first remove any columns that are not needed, such as home addresses if payroll does not use them. I would store the file in a secure network folder that only the HR and payroll staff who need it can open, not on a desktop or a USB stick. The file itself would have a strong password to open, and sheets would be protected so formulas cannot be changed. Hiding columns or using white text is not protection and would not be used. The file would never be sent by ordinary e-mail; if it must be shared, a secure method would be used. Backups would be kept securely. Access would be reviewed when staff change roles. When the data is no longer needed, it would be deleted securely, as the retention policy sets.
markingPoints: Recognises the data as personal and sensitive and states the law's general aims
Collects only what is needed
Limits access with secure storage and passwords, and protects sheets
Avoids weak methods such as hiding columns, and shares securely
Keeps backups, reviews access and deletes data as policy sets

essays.stem: Explain how you would combine monthly figures from four branch sheets into a company summary, and how you would manage the risks.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first make sure all four branch sheets use the same template, with the same cost lines in the same rows and the same headings, ideally locked so branches cannot change the layout. If the branches are sheets in one workbook, the summary can use formulas such as =Kingston!F20+MoBay!F20, or a 3-D sum across the sheets, or SUMIFS on a combined table. If they are separate files, I would either link to them with external references or, better, import each branch's data into one table and summarise it with SUMIFS or a pivot table. The risks are links breaking when files are moved or renamed, branches sending late or wrong data, layouts changing so that formulas pick up the wrong cells, and old figures being shown without anyone noticing. To manage them I would keep files in fixed shared folders, use a submission deadline and a checklist, add control totals and check cells that compare the summary with each branch's own total, show the date of each branch's data, and keep a log of each month's version.
markingPoints: Uses a common, locked template for every branch
Describes suitable methods: sheet references, 3-D sums, SUMIFS or a combined table
Identifies the risks: broken links, late data, layout changes, stale figures
Uses control totals and check cells to confirm the summary
Manages files, deadlines and versions

essays.stem: Evaluate using a macro to automate the preparation of a monthly sales report in a spreadsheet.
essays.modelAnswer: A macro records or codes a set of steps, such as importing the month's data, removing blank rows, applying formats, refreshing a pivot table and printing the report, so they run with one click. The benefits are saved time each month, the same steps done the same way every time, fewer manual errors and less need for one skilled person to be present. However, there are drawbacks. Macro-enabled files can carry harmful code, so many organisations block them and staff must only open macros from trusted sources. A recorded macro may fail if the data's layout, sheet names or number of rows change, and it may do the wrong thing without warning. Few staff may understand how to fix or update it, which creates a key-person risk. Macros can also make a workbook harder to audit. I would recommend using a macro if the report is produced often and the data layout is stable, provided the macro is tested with sample data, documented on a notes sheet, stored in a trusted location, approved under the IT policy and checked each month against control totals.
markingPoints: Explains what a macro does in this task
Gives benefits: time, consistency, fewer manual errors
Identifies security risks of macro-enabled files
Identifies the risks of failure, poor maintainability and auditing
Makes a justified recommendation with safeguards

essays.stem: A growing business keeps all its customer orders in one large spreadsheet used by eight staff. Evaluate whether it should keep the spreadsheet or move to a database or business system.
essays.modelAnswer: The spreadsheet is cheap, familiar and flexible, and staff can quickly sort, filter and chart the data. For a small number of users and records it works well. However, with eight staff using one file, problems grow: people overwrite each other's work or save different copies, there is no proper record of who changed what, and validation is easy to bypass, so data errors creep in. Large files become slow, formulas can be broken by one wrong edit, and personal data is hard to protect at the level of individual users. A database or business system, such as an order or customer management system, stores each order once, allows many users at the same time, controls who can see and change what, keeps an audit trail and links orders to stock and invoices. Its drawbacks are cost, set-up time, training and less flexibility for ad hoc analysis. I would recommend moving the orders into a suitable business system, then exporting data to a spreadsheet for analysis and charts, which uses the strengths of both.
markingPoints: Gives the strengths of the spreadsheet
Identifies the problems of many users sharing one large spreadsheet
Notes data quality, audit and security weaknesses
Explains the benefits and drawbacks of a database or business system
Makes a justified recommendation, such as a system with spreadsheets for analysis

essays.stem: A company pays sales commission of 3% on monthly sales up to J$1,000,000 and 5% on the whole amount if sales are above J$1,000,000, but only if the salesperson has no unresolved complaints. Explain how you would set this up in a spreadsheet, giving example formulas.
essays.modelAnswer: I would put each salesperson on a row, with sales in column B and the number of unresolved complaints in column C. The two rates and the J$1,000,000 threshold would go in labelled input cells, for example F1 for the threshold, F2 for 3% and F3 for 5%, so they can be changed without editing formulas. In D2 I would use a nested IF. In words it reads: if the complaints in C2 are more than zero, pay 0; otherwise, if the sales in B2 are more than the threshold in $F$1, pay B2 times $F$3, and if not, pay B2 times $F$2. AND can be used instead to test both conditions in one step. The absolute references keep the formula pointing to the input cells when it is copied down. I would wrap the result in ROUND to two decimal places. An alternative is a lookup to a small rate table using an approximate match on sales bands, which is easier to extend if more bands are added. I would test it with cases at, below and above J$1,000,000, with and without complaints; for example, J$1,200,000 with no complaints should give J$60,000.
markingPoints: Lays out the data with rates and threshold in labelled input cells
Gives a correct nested IF that handles complaints and the two rates
Uses absolute references so the formula copies correctly
Mentions rounding or a lookup-table alternative
Tests with cases at, below and above the threshold, with a correct example

practical1.title: Build a budget-against-actual workbook with lookups, conditional totals, flags, a chart and protection
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a data pack for a made-up Jamaican business (for example a guest house or a hardware store): a list of departments and cost codes, the approved monthly budget and three months of actual spending exported as a CSV file. As a group, build one workbook on a Centre computer. Give each member a named role: designer (plans the sheets and builds the settings sheet with named cells and a drop-down list of departments), data officer (imports and cleans the actuals, using TRIM or similar, and formats them as a table), formula builder (builds the summary with SUMIF or SUMIFS, a lookup (VLOOKUP or XLOOKUP) for department names, the variance and percentage, and an IF flag for lines more than 10% over budget), chart and format lead (adds conditional formatting and a clear chart of budget against actual by department), and tester (tests the workbook with known figures, checks control totals, unlocks the input cells, protects the sheets and writes the notes sheet). In a group of four, the designer also does the testing. Take a screen photo at each stage.
materials: Data pack and CSV file from the assessor
A USB drive or shared folder set up by the Centre for saving the work
photos: The settings sheet with named cells and the drop-down list
The summary sheet showing the formulas in use (formula view) and the results
Conditional formatting flagging lines over budget, and the chart
The tester's record of test figures and control totals
The protected sheet and the notes sheet
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the workbook
Uses absolute or named references correctly so formulas copy without errors
SUMIF/SUMIFS, the lookup and the IF flag give correct results
Imported data is cleaned and control totals agree with the data pack
Chart is the right type, clearly labelled and honest
Input cells are unlocked, the rest protected, and the notes sheet explains the workbook
Can explain their formulas to the assessor
safety: Save work only to the folder or drive the Centre provides; do not e-mail files outside the Centre
Treat the data pack as confidential business information
Sit well, set the screen at eye level and take a short break at least every hour
Share the keyboard fairly and help members who are less confident

practical2.title: Analyse a year of sales data with a pivot table and dashboard, and present the findings
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a spreadsheet of one year's sales for a made-up business with several branches (date, branch, product group, salesperson code, quantity and value), with some deliberate problems: extra spaces, inconsistent branch names, text stored as numbers and a few duplicate rows. As a group, clean the data, analyse it and present a one-page dashboard to the assessor, playing the managing director. Give each member a named role: data cleaner (finds and fixes the data problems and records each fix), pivot builder (builds pivot tables of sales by branch and month and by product group, and refreshes them after cleaning), formula analyst (uses SUMIFS, COUNTIFS and a lookup to work out each branch's growth and average sale and checks them against the pivot tables), dashboard designer (builds the dashboard with two or three charts and key figures), and presenter (presents three findings and one recommendation in 10 minutes). In a group of four, the formula analyst also presents. Take a screen photo at each stage.
materials: Sales data spreadsheet from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and presentation software
A shared folder set up by the Centre for saving the work
photos: The data cleaner's log of problems found and fixed
The pivot tables of sales by branch and month and by product group
The formula check that agrees with the pivot table totals
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the work
Found and fixed the data problems and recorded each fix
Pivot tables are correct and refreshed after cleaning
Formula results agree with the pivot tables
Dashboard charts are suitable, labelled and easy to read
Findings are supported by the data and the recommendation is sensible
safety: Save work only to the shared folder the Centre provides
Treat the sales data as confidential and do not copy it to personal devices
Sit well and take a short screen break at least every hour
Respect each other's ideas and share the work fairly
